title: Aspirin: The Wonder Drug
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of aspirin, from willow bark remedies in ancient Sumer and Egypt, through salicylic acid isolation, Edward Stone's 1763 willow bark study, and the German chemists at Bayer who made synthetic aspirin (with the disputed credit of Felix Hoffman, Arthur Eichengrün, and Heinrich Dreser). They cover the trademark and patent history, Bayer's tablet and cotton-ball packaging, the World War One phenol embargo and Thomas Edison sale, the discovery of how aspirin works via prostaglandins and COX enzymes, its shift to blood thinner and preventive use for heart attack and stroke, possible cancer benefits, Reye's syndrome in children, and modern formulations. The episode also includes off-topic banter about Josh's book, headache powders, and a listener mail segment about a Bay of Pigs film.
topics: low dose aspirin heart attack prevention

segments.title: Opening banter and headache powders
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about headache powders such as Goody's and BC, the taste of aspirin, and Josh's new book, and introduce aspirin as the most-sold drug in history.

segments.title: Willow bark and ancient remedies
segments.summary: The hosts describe willow bark as an early remedy used by the Sumerians and Egyptians, with salicylic acid as its active ingredient, and mention the Ebers Papyrus.

segments.title: Cinchona, Edward Stone, and isolating salicylic acid
segments.summary: Cinchona bark was used for malaria but was expensive to import. Reverend Edward Stone studied willow bark in 1763 as an alternative, and later chemists isolated salicylic acid, which occurs in many plants.

segments.title: Gerhardt and synthetic salicylates
segments.summary: A French chemist, Gerhardt, made an impure early version of aspirin by accident. German chemists later learned the structure of salicylate and produced it synthetically, making it cheap and popular despite stomach side effects.

segments.title: Bayer and the invention of aspirin
segments.summary: Bayer, a dye company that started a pharmaceutical division, sought a gentler version of salicylate. Felix Hoffman's August 10 notebook entry is cited as the invention, with competing claims from Arthur Eichengrün and Heinrich Dreser, and Carl Duisberg's marketing role noted.

segments.title: Aspirin trademark, patents, and World War One
segments.summary: The name aspirin is explained as a combination of acetyl and Spiraea. Germany lost its patents after World War One, retaining only some trademarks. England embargoed phenol, and Thomas Edison reportedly sold phenol to Germany during the war.
topics: patent surrender after World War One

segments.title: Tablets, cotton balls, and aspirin sales
segments.summary: Bayer helped popularize compressed aspirin tablets and introduced the cotton ball in pill bottles. The hosts discuss aspirin sales figures and its popularity in Argentina.

segments.title: How aspirin works: prostaglandins and COX enzymes
segments.summary: Researchers in the late 1960s and early 1970s, including John Vane, found that aspirin blocks prostaglandin release by inhibiting cyclooxygenase enzymes, which earned Vane a Nobel Prize. Advil is compared as a reversible alternative.

segments.title: Blood thinning and heart attack prevention
segments.summary: Lawrence Craven noticed patients who took aspirin bled more during surgery, revealing its blood-thinning effect. Aspirin's role shifted toward preventing clots, heart attacks, and strokes, with cautions about bleeding and talking to a doctor first.

segments.title: Other uses, cancer, Reye's syndrome, and newer formulations
segments.summary: Aspirin is linked to possible reductions in colorectal cancer and dementia, use in transplants, and a warning about Reye's syndrome in children. Bayer's later IG Farben ownership and newer formulations are also covered.

segments.title: Listener mail: Bay of Pigs film
segments.summary: A listener writes about the film Red Zone, Cuba, a Coleman Francis movie partly about the Bay of Pigs, and plugs his artwork. The hosts also correct a Roberto Clemente discharge misstatement.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode and invite listeners to send email.
